item.title: Near-Optimal Sample Complexity of Deterministic Agnostic PAC Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.13210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of agnostic PAC learning under deterministic labels, where the examples are labeled by an arbitrary deterministic function, which need not belong to the concept class $C$. This model captures misspecification without stochastic label noise and lies between the realizable and fully agnostic settings. Prior work showed that, when $C$ has finite diameter $K$ and VC dimension $d$, deterministic labels can improve the sample complexity upper bound from the classical agnostic guarantee $O(d/\varepsilon^2)$ to $\widetilde{O}(K/\varepsilon)$, but left a large gap between upper and lower bounds. Our main result sharpens this picture. We prove that every class of VC dimension $d$ and finite diameter $K$ is learnable with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left( \frac{K^{1/3} \, d^{2/3}}{\varepsilon} \right)$, and we construct classes for which this bound is tight up to logarithmic factors. We also study the online analogue of this problem and show that the minimax regret is again partly controlled by the diameter of the class. Technically, our upper bounds are obtained via memorization-based learning algorithms that exploit the deterministic label structure.
item.dc:creator: Shai Ben-David, Steve Hanneke, Farnam Mansouri, Amirreza Shaeiri

item.title: MediPFN: Amortized In-Context Nuisance Learning and Inference for Causal Mediation Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.13219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Causal mediation analysis decomposes a treatment effect into indirect pathways through mediators and direct pathways through other processes. Tabular foundation models perform classification and regression through in-context learning, providing estimates of conditional means and propensity scores used in causal mediation analysis. Constructing confidence intervals from these estimates requires accounting for uncertainty introduced by fitting and combining several nuisance functions. We introduce MediPFN, an amortized inference framework that adapts a pretrained tabular foundation model to nuisance prediction and combines its predictions through a cross-fitted influence-function estimator. A separate head learns quantiles of the estimator's standardized error from simulated tables with known indirect effects. Supervised fine-tuning, symmetrization, and independent calibration then produce a confidence interval. We establish coverage bounds for the resulting intervals under standard assumptions. Across experiments, MediPFN attains coverage closer to the nominal level than several comparators. It also reduces the computational cost of uncertainty quantification, running 59.1 times faster than bootstrap in matched comparisons.
item.dc:creator: Shi Bo, Jiaming Hu

item.title: Continuous Horizon Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2611.13228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-horizon forecasting has been dominated by discrete forecast strategies that treat model outputs as fixed-vectors or recurrently create them. In this paper, we introduce the Continuous Horizon (CH) strategy that generalizes upon recursive, direct, and multi-step strategies by redefining forecasts as a continuous operator and the forecast horizon as a query variable rather than an index. We present the theoretical foundations for the CH strategy, a Universal Operator Approximation Theorem, and a continuous-horizon bias-variance decomposition that formally proves the estimation variance improvements of CH over the discrete strategies. We validate the CH strategy empirically through a simulation study, and on 16 large-scale datasets from the M-series benchmark, showing how CH achieves competitive RMSE accuracy, while uniquely enabling parallel inference, targeted horizon querying, and interpolation and extrapolation across unseen horizons.
item.dc:creator: Malcolm Wolff, Elliott Zackrone, Souhaib Ben Taieb, Michael W. Mahoney, Kin G. Olivares

item.title: Time Series Change Point Detection with Gaussian Processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.13295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a novel general Gaussian process framework for change point detection in time series. A change is defined as an alteration of the hyperparameters of the Gaussian process prior. We formulate the problem in the context of statistical hypothesis testing and demonstrate its performance over both offline and online multiple change points detection. The approach provides theoretical guaranties of its performance. An important advantage of the developed framework is that it does not need a detailed specification of the time series function before and after a change. The hyperparameter values are learned from the data. Comprehensive evaluation of the proposed framework is provided both on synthetic and real data and its efficiency is demonstrated.
item.dc:creator: Olga Isupova, Danil Kuzin, Fredrik Gustafsson, Lyudmila Mihaylova

item.title: VC-Dimension and Generalization in Geometric Machine Learning with Applications to Active Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.13337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We compute the VC-dimension of metric ball classifiers in the model spaces of Riemannian geometry (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) and present upper and lower bounds on the VC-dimension of metric balls in several other situations, including general normed vector spaces (potentially infinite VC-dimension), vector spaces with $\ell^p$-norms (VC-dimension grows at least linearly in the dimension, faster than Euclidean for $p=1$), flat tori, and general Riemannian manifolds (arbitrarily large VC-dimension after a conformal change). In several situations where the VC-dimension is large or even infinite, we prove generalization bounds under additional assumptions on the data distribution using covering arguments. Both in the VC-dimension and covering setting, we consider data on low-dimensional subsets of high-dimensional Euclidean spaces. As an application, we consider coverage-based algorithms in active learning.
item.dc:creator: Gokul Bhusal, Delanna Do, Ekaterina Merkurjev, Kevin Miller, Stephan Wojtowytsch

item.title: Differentially Private Statistical Inference for Rankings from Pairwise Comparisons
item.description: arXiv:2611.13485v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable inference for rankings of large language models based on human pairwise comparisons must preserve the privacy of individual preference records. To meet this need, we develop methods for score and rank inference under the Bradley-Terry model with edge differential privacy. For an objective-perturbed estimator, a new leave-one-out analysis establishes finite-sample bounds on Euclidean and entrywise estimation errors. For sufficiently dense comparison graphs, the error bounds extend to smaller privacy budgets, including regimes in which its privacy term dominates its statistical term. A uniform asymptotic expansion yields asymptotically valid confidence intervals for individual scores and pairwise score differences. To improve finite-sample performance, we account for both regularization bias and privacy-induced randomness by combining a plug-in ridge-bias correction with Gaussian-Laplace calibration. We further establish a bootstrap procedure for simultaneous rank inference, providing asymptotically valid confidence sets for individual ranks and tests of top-$K$ membership. When the comparison probability is public and known, all proposed inferential procedures require no additional privacy budget. We evaluate finite-sample performance through simulations and apply the proposed methods to rank large language models for creative writing.
item.dc:creator: Xintao Xia, Jia Gu

item.title: Simultaneous Near-Optimal Region Identification in Continuous Simulation Optimization: Minimax Complexity and Adaptive Sampling
item.description:
arXiv:2611.13489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulation optimization typically returns a single estimated optimal point. When decisions also depend on criteria evaluated independently of simulation, such as resource cost, the decision maker instead needs the set of designs whose expected performance lies within a tolerance of the optimum, often choosing the tolerance only after seeing the tradeoffs. We study how to identify these near-optimal regions on a continuous design space, simultaneously for all tolerances up to a prescribed maximum $T$, with region estimation error at most $\eta$. We show that region identification is not a by-product of optimization. Specifically, when $\alpha>
u$, any procedure, even one given the optimal design in advance, needs at least $\Omega igl(\eta^{-(2+d/
u)}\min\{1,KT^{d/\alpha}\} igr)$ simulation evaluations, where $d$ is the dimension, $
u$ the smoothness, and $(K,\alpha)$ the covering parameters that describe the geometry of the near-optimal designs. We propose SASORI, which returns an estimated optimal point and the regions for all tolerances from the same evaluations, matching this lower bound up to logarithmic factors. SASORI also achieves the optimal tradeoff between region estimation error and cumulative regret, and reduces to a minimax-optimal simulation optimization procedure at zero tolerance. Numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Yilin Zheng, Haowei Wang, Wenjia Wang, Szu Hui Ng

item.title: Outliers and the Hard-Margin Linear SVM in High-Dimension, Low-Sample-Size Settings
item.description: arXiv:2611.13869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how outliers affect the hard-margin linear support vector machine when the dimension grows while the sample sizes remain fixed. For one-sided contamination, the centered Gram matrix converges to a constant inlier block plus an outlier-diagonal component, and the limiting dual problem has a closed-form solution. All outliers act through one effective distance. This representation yields explicit thresholds for loss of inlier support, margin shrinkage. intercept displacement, and asymptotic misclassification. We then treat contamination in both classes. The limiting intercept is the multiplier of the class-balance constraint, and the two classes pull it in opposite directions. Consequently, at most one class can collapse or be asymptotically misclassified, whereas symmetric contamination leaves the limiting discriminant function unchanged even though the margin shrinks. Seven numerical experiments verify the dual allocation, phase transitions, and discriminant limits.
item.dc:creator: Yugo Nakayama

item.title: On the Spectral Estimation of VARMA Processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.13973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the power spectral density of a Vector-valued Autoregressive Moving-Average (VARMA) process. A well-established approach to accomplishing this task consists of formulating a moment problem that selects the spectral density maximizing an entropy-like index while matching certain moments of the underlying process. However, existing methods assume that the moving-average (MA) component is either fixed or scalar, thereby reducing the class of ARMA models over which the optimal spectral density is sought. In this paper, we propose a new moment problem, based on the notion of transportation entropy, for learning the spectral density of a VARMA process without fixing the MA component or restricting it to be scalar.
item.dc:creator: Bin Zhu, Mattia Zorzi

item.title: Compositional random forest
item.description: arXiv:2611.14275v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compositional data have been analysed in the literature from three main points of view: directly on the simplex, in log-ratio coordinates, and as directional data on the unit sphere. In this paper, we construct a random forest framework for compositional responses that accommodates all three. Random forests are ensembles of decision trees, and the split criterion determines how each tree grows. We use the log-likelihood gain as the split criterion and consider distributions defined on the different spaces in which compositions can be represented. The Dirichlet likelihood has been studied in the literature, but its covariance is fixed by its mean up to a single scalar, and its maximum likelihood estimator has no closed form. To obtain more flexible criteria, we use two well-known transformations. First, the square-root transformation maps compositions onto the unit sphere, where existing directional distributions require numerical estimation. We introduce a tangent-normal (TN) distribution, which shares its parameters with the Kent distribution, and construct a split criterion whose gain is computed from additive sufficient statistics: the shape parameters are maximised out in closed form, up to an exponentially small truncation constant, so that no parameter is estimated iteratively. Second, the log-ratio transformation maps compositions to Euclidean space, where the multivariate logistic-normal distribution has a flexible covariance and a closed-form maximum log-likelihood, also based on additive sufficient statistics. Both criteria respond to a shift of the mean, measured relative to the covariance, and to a change in the covariance itself. In simulations, the most accurate forest depended on the covariance structure of the composition. The TN forest was the most accurate in two of the three designs.
item.dc:creator: Khaled Masoumifard, Stephan van der Westhuizen, Sugnet Gardner-Lubbe

item.title: A Theory of Cross-Validation Variance
item.description: arXiv:2611.14463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross-validation estimates predictive performance by repeatedly splitting the data into training and validation sets, fitting the model on the first and evaluating it on the second. Every observation influences the estimate in two roles, through its own evaluation when it is held out and through the models it helps fit when it trains. The random splits determine its weight in each role. From this representation, we prove an exact finite-sample identity for the variance of the cross-validated estimate. For a given splitting scheme with a common training set size, the variance is a function of these weights, with constants of the model, the metric, and the population. It covers metrics averaged over observations, such as mean squared error, and over case--control pairs, such as the AUC. The identity shows which schemes to use. The variance decomposes into sampling variance, which depends only on the training size, and variance due to the random fold splitting, which arises when the weights change from one draw of the splits to the next. K-fold cross-validation, whose weights are equal across observations by design, is therefore variance optimal at first order; Monte Carlo and bootstrap cross-validation are not. The first-order variance of K-fold does not depend on K, and under reasonable conditions on the model leave-one-out has the smallest variance of any K-fold scheme. For the AUC the same holds for leave-pair-out, which evaluates every case--control pair. Finally, we show the cross-validated estimate is asymptotically normal with the identity's full variance. Together, these results provide a general theoretical foundation for inference on cross-validated performance and establish principles for selecting variance-optimal cross-validation designs.
item.dc:creator: Nathaniel S. O'Connell, Jaime L. Speiser

item.title: Geometry and Stochastic Analysis of Flow and Diffusion Models: A Survey
item.description: arXiv:2611.12107v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Flow-based and diffusion-based models have become the principal means of learning and sampling high-dimensional probability distributions, from images and video to proteins, molecules and physical fields, and increasingly language. Each carries a simple law to the law of the data along a curve of probability measures, and behind the variety of their names lie three geometries, those of the state space on which the data live, of the space of probability measures through which the curve passes, and of the space of paths traced by the generating process. A single analytic idea runs through the subject. Every score identity used to train a diffusion model is an integration by parts, on the noise, on the data or on Wiener space, and Malliavin calculus extends this to nonlinear and infinite-dimensional diffusions. We develop these foundations with full definitions and follow them through normalising flows, flow matching and few-step maps, diffusion models and their convergence theory, conditioning, Schr\"odinger bridges and stochastic control, and their extension to manifolds, Lie groups, discrete and function spaces and jump processes. We close with statistical physics, renormalisation and, more speculatively, holography, in which the radial direction of anti-de Sitter space can play the role of flow time. A table of the main methods and a collection of open problems complete the survey.
item.dc:creator: Ehsan Mirafzali, Razvan Marinescu

item.title: Generative Learning on Manifolds for Probabilistic Seismic Performance Assessment and Structural Identifiability
item.description: arXiv:2611.12908v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Seismic performance assessment relies on computationally expensive nonlinear simulations, limiting uncertainty quantification and inference of structural properties from observed responses. We develop a manifold-based generative framework that learns the joint distribution of uncertain structural parameters and seismic-response trajectories from limited high-fidelity simulations. Combining Diffusion Maps, score-based Diffusion Modeling, and Geometric Harmonics, the framework enables both forward probabilistic prediction and inverse inference. Applied to a nine-story steel moment-resisting frame, the results reveal which structural properties are identifiable from seismic performance and how uncertainty in these properties influences response. In particular, the learned representation captures post-capping degradation characteristics more effectively than individual strength parameters. Inverse inference identifies distinct structural configurations that produce similar seismic performance, with representative solutions independently validated using nonlinear simulations. These findings demonstrate how generative learning can support uncertainty-aware seismic assessment while revealing structural non-identifiability and alternative mechanisms underlying observed performance
item.dc:creator: Dimitris G Giovanis, Ioannis G Kevrekidis, Roger G Ghanem

item.title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series
item.description: arXiv:2611.12955v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without a single annotation, language model call, or domain expert. Code is available at: https://github.com/Sachithx/ConceptTime.git.
item.dc:creator: Sachith Abeywickrama, Emadeldeen Eldele, Min Wu, Xiaoli Li, Chau Yuen

item.title: Prediction Inference for Hybrid Models on Realized Volatility Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2611.13212v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GARCH-LSTM hybrid models have become increasingly popular in the volatility forecasting literature. To date, these models have almost exclusively focused on point estimation and accuracy measures such as RMSE and MAPE, while failing to assess the uncertainty of these point estimates. We approach this gap in two ways. First, we extend the existing GARCH-LSTM model by modeling the conditional mean with an ARMA structure. Second, we develop a forward bootstrap algorithm to build multi-step-ahead prediction intervals for future realized volatility. In order to address the notorious undercoverage of prediction intervals, we implement two solutions. One draws bootstrap innovations from the empirical residual distribution to mimic the fat-tail property of financial series. The other utilizes principles from conformal prediction to systematically extend the prediction interval length. We evaluate the methods in simulations with heavy-tailed and time-varying GARCH processes and in rolling-window forecasts of four U.S. stock indices from 2020 to 2025. The ARMA-based hybrid gives the lowest point-forecast errors in most settings, and combining both remedies with the mean-based hybrid yields intervals closest to the nominal level among competing methods.
item.dc:creator: Kyle Parrella, Kejin Wu

item.title: Settling the Burn-in Gap: Sharp Risk Bounds for Tail-Averaged SGD in Linear Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.13383v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the excess risk of constant-stepsize online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with tail-averaging for high-dimensional linear regression. Building on the instance-dependent spectral framework of Zou et al. (2021), we establish matching initialization-explicit upper and lower bounds on the total excess risk of tail-averaged SGD in terms of the population covariance spectrum $\mathbf{H}$ and initialization $\mathbf{w}_0-\mathbf{w}^*$ whenever a trajectory spectral feedback condition holds. Existing analyses exhibit a fundamental gap in the effective variance: the upper bound of Zou et al. (2021) retains an undamped contribution from the initial error in the head eigenspace $\mathbf{I}_{0:k^\dagger}$, whereas their lower bound omits the variance induced by the head initialization altogether. We show that both the existing upper and lower bounds are loose: the single-hop fast-mode variance contribution from the head initialization is exponentially damped during the burn-in phase, whereas fourth-moment energy scattered from the head initialization into slow spectral modes during the early burn-in steps survives undamped into the averaging window. We prove that our spectral feedback condition is satisfied in two concrete constant-stepsize regimes: (i) for arbitrary covariance spectra $\mathbf{H}$ and any finite horizon, under an explicit horizon-dependent stepsize chosen prior to execution; and (ii) for polynomially decaying spectra $\lambda_i\asymp i^{-a}$ ($a>1$), under a single horizon-independent positive stepsize. Finally, we complement these positive results with explicit one- and two-dimensional separation constructions proving an exponential-versus-polynomial gap in the lower bound of Zou et al. (2021) and showing why fourth-moment assumptions alone cannot determine the asymptotic exponential decay rate without additional structural conditions.
item.dc:creator: Qingyue Zhao, Xuheng Li, Quanquan Gu

item.title: Sufficient Dimension Reduction with Multimodal Predictor Objects
item.description: arXiv:2611.13460v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the regression of a scalar response $Y$ on a Euclidean predictor $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and a random predictor object $\mathcal{Z}$ in a general metric space under arbitrary structural dependence. We introduce a joint sufficient dimension reduction $(\mathbf{B}^\top\mathbf{X}, \mathcal{G}_Z)$ constructed via a sequential conditional independence framework, which differs fundamentally from the ordinary central subspace of $Y \mid \mathbf{X}$. Methodologically, $\mathcal{Z}$ is embedded into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and a regularized kernel-response envelope model extracts a finite-dimensional reduction of the feature map. Partial adaptive estimation then recovers the Euclidean reduction conditional on the first-stage coordinates. We establish root-$n$ consistency rates for the first-stage envelope subspace under a shrinking regularizer, alongside large-sample consistency for the second-stage Euclidean subspace estimator. Simulations and two real-data applications illustrate the utility and flexibility of the proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Abdul-Nasah Soale

item.title: Closing the BF16-FP16 Convergence Speed Gap in RL Post-Training with Stochastic Rounding
item.description: arXiv:2611.13545v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: BF16 is widely used to pretrain large language models because it has the same dynamic range as FP32 and converges similarly to FP32 training. However, in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where learning rates are typically low, we find that standard mixed-precision BF16 training converges more slowly than FP16 training at the same learning rate. We attribute this gap to weight sticking: when FP32 shadow weights are quantized to BF16 using round-to-nearest, small updates often leave the BF16 weights used for rollout generation and training unchanged. Consequently, several optimizer steps may be needed before updates to the shadow weights are reflected in the BF16 weights. Raising the BF16 learning rate reduces weight sticking and matches FP16's convergence speed, but it also increases the KL divergence from the reference model. We instead apply stochastic rounding when quantizing the FP32 shadow weights to BF16. This approach matches FP16's convergence speed across different models and datasets while reducing the KL divergence relative to BF16 training with a larger learning rate. Unlike FP16, it keeps BF16's wider dynamic range and needs no loss scaling.
item.dc:creator: Mahdi Nazemi, Oleg Rybakov, Tijmen Blankevoort, Asit Mishra, Carlo del Mundo

item.title: Investigating Composite Modeling in Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization for Scientific Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.13565v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scientific design often requires balancing competing objectives that are expensive to evaluate through experiments or simulations. Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) addresses this challenge by using probabilistic models to guide the selection of promising designs. In many applications, tunable inputs map to observable intermediate responses, which are then combined through known functions to compute the final objectives. Prior work on Bayesian optimization of composite functions shows that learning from these intermediate responses, which we call Composite modeling, can substantially improve sampling efficiency in single-objective optimization, compared to methods that condition only on black-box observations of the objective function. The benefits of Composite modeling in MOBO, however, remain understudied. In this work, we study the benefits of Composite modeling in MOBO and investigate the factors driving variation in its gains. We first establish single-objective conditions under which intermediate observations provide no additional predictive information beyond objective values, where composite and black box methods use the same warped Gaussian process prior. Controlled numerical experiments with versions of four MOBO methods across eight synthetic and application-inspired scientific-design benchmarks examine how these conditions relate to optimization gains in the multi-objective setting, where the black box approach models the objective functions with a standard multi-output Gaussian process. Both investigations support the claim that composite modeling tends to help more when the function mapping intermediate responses to final objectives is non-bijective and non-affine.
item.dc:creator: Ricky Ye, Sahas Goli, Muhammad Ali, Poompol Buathong, Peter I. Frazier

item.title: First-order asymptotic expansions for spectral convergence of normalized graph Laplacians constructed from samples on manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2611.13623v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Under i.i.d. uniform sampling from a closed Riemannian manifold embedded in Euclidean space, we derive first-order asymptotic expansions for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetrically normalized graph Laplacians constructed via Gaussian kernels and provide concentration inequalities for the remainder terms. As a direct consequence, we establish the corresponding weak convergence results. Unlike most related works, our analysis does not impose a multiplicity-one assumption on the eigenvalues, thereby extending the applicability of the framework to general manifolds with potentially nontrivial eigenvalue multiplicities.
item.dc:creator: Eunseong Bae, Wolfgang Polonik

item.title: CP-MLPs: A Tensor-Rank Theory of Tied and Untied MLP Blocks
item.description: arXiv:2611.13647v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transformer feed-forward blocks combine several design choices: squared activations, gating, and tied versus untied parameter sharing, whose separate contributions to expressivity remain poorly understood. We introduce CP-MLPs, a tensor framework in which each multiplicative unit contributes a rank-1 interaction with three roles: detecting an input feature, reading a value, and writing to the output. Tied gated blocks such as ReLU$^2$ force the detector and value roles to share the same direction; untied gated blocks such as ReGLU and SwiGLU let them differ. We show that this distinction yields exact, degree-wise tensor-rank separations: untied detector-value units are strictly more width-efficient for indefinite quadratic interactions and role-asymmetric monomials, while tied units are structurally matched to symmetric pure-power targets. The width advantage of untying therefore depends on the target structure. Experiments show loss plateaus below the exact-representation width, but these plateaus alone do not establish a positive approximation gap: arbitrarily accurate approximation is governed by border rank. In trained gated MLPs, untied blocks retain an advantage in selected comparisons at matched input-projection budget. Code is available at https://github.com/rarefin/CP-MLPs.
item.dc:creator: Md Rifat Arefin, Farzaneh Heidari, Irina Rish, Guillaume Rabusseau

item.title: Beyond Interaction Scores: Selecting Feature Interactions via Independent Replication
item.description: arXiv:2611.13765v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learning feature interactions is essential for accurate prediction and interpretable modeling, yet a high interaction score may reflect fitting noise rather than a reproducible pattern. Ranking methods score feature pairs but leave the cutoff to the user; testing methods set the cutoff but rely on repeated model refits or a model of the joint feature distribution. We present LENS, a model-agnostic framework for selecting feature interactions through independent replication. LENS trains two models with the same learning algorithm on disjoint data and accesses them only through predictions. For each feature pair, it removes main effects from the joint-effect surface to isolate an interaction pattern, ranks pairs by its strength, and tests whether the second model reproduces it at a meaningful strength. A single multiple-testing correction determines which pairs to retain, using only two model fits regardless of the number of features. We prove that a replication ratio alone can retain arbitrarily weak patterns shared by both fits, whereas a strength floor restores selection consistency, and we characterize when normalization in Friedman's $H^2$ reverses interaction rankings. On 16 synthetic designs, LENS matches leading model-specific ranking methods (e.g., TreeSHAP) and recovers 91% of material interactions, against 45% for the knockoff-based DIAMOND, without selecting false pairs; with 1,225 candidate pairs and no interactions, it makes substantially fewer false discoveries. On large-scale French motor insurance data, it identifies interactions documented in the actuarial literature and recovers 90% of the deviance gain obtained using all pairs. On two credit datasets, LENS selects few pairs while maintaining or slightly improving predictive performance over the additive baseline.
item.dc:creator: Jincheng Gao, Shuo Sun

item.title: MEOW: Medical Open-World Interactive Segmentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.13935v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In open-world recognition, machine learning models not only make predictions on unknown structures ("generalized open-set"), but also continually learn and improve from those predictions over time. Interactive segmentation, despite its access to user feedback, has so far remained confined to the open-set setting. In this work we introduce MEOW, the first framework that turns non-interactive segmentation backbones into interactive open-world learners without updating learnable model parameters. MEOW combines parameter-free transductive reasoning with memory consolidation to accumulate knowledge and thereby improve future performance. Focusing on medical data, we show that MEOW consistently improves its own predictions on classes never seen during training, and transfers zero-shot to unfamiliar domains, including micro-CT data and other imaging modalities.
item.dc:creator: Philip Matthias Winter, Maria Wimmer, Bernhard Sch\"{a}fl, David Major, Dimitrios Lenis, Astrid Berg, Theresa Neubauer, Ariharasudhan Muthusami, Johannes Novotny, Georg Zotti, Katja B\"{u}hler

item.title: Forward-Value Discretization: Faster Stochastic Diffusion Sampling Without High-Order Approximation
item.description: arXiv:2611.14328v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stochastic diffusion samplers often require substantially more neural function evaluations (NFEs) than deterministic samplers to achieve comparable sample quality. Although higher-order discretization accelerates deterministic sampling, its benefits for stochastic sampling remains unclear. We establish matching upper and worst-case lower bounds showing that stochastic samplers with higher-order approximations remain first-order convergent, even with exact score functions. Thus, increasing the approximation order does not generally improve the convergence order. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce forward-value discretization, a training-free framework that evaluates the data/noise prediction model at a lookahead estimate constructed from previous predictions. For deterministic sampling, the resulting Forward DPMSolver (F-DPMSolver), improves sample quality at low NFE budgets through its DDIM-based variant, despite remaining first-order convergent. For stochastic sampling, we develop Forward DDPM (F-DDPM), which evaluates the model at a cleaner lookahead point adjusted for subsequent noise injection. This estimate reuses both the previous model prediction and the previously injected noise. Both variants admit first-order convergence guarantees with one model evaluation per iteration. Across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, FFHQ, and LSUN, F-DDPM consistently achieves lower FID than the evaluated stochastic baselines at matched NFE budgets. With 1.5 times as many NFEs as deterministic baselines, it achieves competitive sample quality, narrowing the practical efficiency gap between stochastic and deterministic sampling. Code is available at https://github.com/Na-Li66/F-DDPM.
item.dc:creator: Yuchen Jiao, Na Li, Changxiao Cai, Yuting Wei, Gen Li

item.title: Nonparametric Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Mixtures of Logistic Regressions
item.description: arXiv:2611.14445v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mixtures of logistic regressions provide a flexible framework for modeling binary responses, extending standard logistic regression to accommodate unobserved heterogeneity while retaining an interpretable regression structure. In this paper, we study such models with an unspecified mixing distribution. We analyze a sieve nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) and derive nonasymptotic bounds on the estimation error of the resulting mixture regression function under both fixed and random designs. Our results reveal an explicit tradeoff between statistical estimation error and the approximation error induced by the sieve radius, from which we derive convergence rates under several tail conditions on the mixing distribution. For computation, we propose a finite-particle algorithm that approximates the sieve NPMLE by optimizing the locations and weights of a finitely supported mixing distribution. The method offers numerical advantages over existing algorithms and comes with rigorous convergence guarantees. For any fixed dataset, we establish global convergence of the likelihood to the restricted NPMLE value when the number of particles exceeds a finite threshold. When the true mixing distribution is finitely supported, we further establish uniform global convergence guarantees and derive error bounds that separate algorithmic and statistical errors. Our analysis also yields a denoising bound for the mixing distribution and an identifiability result that complements existing results in the literature.
item.dc:creator: Muheng Li, Peize Zhang, Xin Bing

item.title: One Curve, Different Weights: AUC, the Brier Score, Decision-Weighted AUC, and the Policy Youden Index
item.description: arXiv:2611.14465v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AUC and the Brier score are standard summaries of a binary risk score, yet they can rank models differently. We introduce a weighted AUC, AUC$_\pi$, which weights each pair of observations by how differently a decision maker with probability of acting $\pi$ treats them. We show that all three are built on weighted averages of one curve, the Youden index $J(t) = \mathrm{TPR}(t) - \mathrm{FPR}(t)$ across cutoffs $t$, and that the averages differ in the weights they put on the cutoffs. Each weights a cutoff by how much something rises across it: for AUC, the distribution of all scores; for the Brier score, the true probability $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid S]$; for AUC$_\pi$, the decision maker's probability of acting. Up to normalization, AUC$_\pi$ is the Brier skill score of the ideal forecast with its weight moved to the cutoffs the decision maker cares about. We also show that weighting pairs by $|\pi(s) - \pi(s')|$ is, up to scale, the only pair weight fixed in advance that makes a pair-weighted AUC an average of the Youden curve for every score distribution. As a ranking measure, AUC weights every model the same way. Hand (2009) shows that it can also be read as an average over cost thresholds, and in that reading each model weights the thresholds differently. The numerator of AUC$_\pi$, which we call the policy Youden index, is the expected share of class 1 a fixed policy acts on minus the expected share of class 0. It judges every model by the same policy and so avoids this; the full ratio AUC$_\pi$ does not.
item.dc:creator: Yegor Baranovski

item.title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets
item.description: arXiv:2611.14467v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.
item.dc:creator: Audrey Huang, Nan Jiang, Sham M. Kakade, Sadhika Malladi, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Dylan J. Foster

item.title: TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves
item.description: arXiv:2611.14516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present TorchCurves, a PyTorch library that treats vector-valued parametric curves as learnable primitives. Its central operation maps batches of scalar inputs to points on curves represented in B-spline or Legendre polynomial bases, with differentiation through both inputs and coefficients. Curve coefficients can be optimized jointly with the surrounding model or produced by another network. The library provides trainable modules, reusable basis modules, and a functional interface, supporting applications ranging from continuous feature embeddings to Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and functional regression. Its implementation combines classical evaluation algorithms with vectorized PyTorch operations, emphasizing readability and maintainability without custom hardware kernels. Timing experiments compare curve evaluation against NumPy and SciPy and KAN training against EfficientKAN across a range of problem sizes. The results illustrate where this generality remains computationally practical and where overhead is substantial. Library is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexshtf/torchcurves.
item.dc:creator: Alex Shtoff

item.title: Low-degree lower bounds via almost orthonormal bases
item.description: arXiv:2509.09353v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Low-degree polynomials have emerged as a powerful paradigm for providing evidence of statistical--computational gaps across a variety of high-dimensional statistical models [Wein25]. For detection problems---where the goal is to test a planted distribution $\mathbb{P}'$ against a null distribution $\mathbb{P}$ with independent components---the standard approach is to bound the advantage using an $\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{P})$-orthonormal family of polynomials. However, this method breaks down for estimation tasks or more complex testing problems where $\mathbb{P}$ has some planted structures, so that no simple $\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{P})$-orthogonal polynomial family is available. To address this challenge, several technical workarounds have been proposed [SW22,SW25], though their implementation can be delicate. In this work, we propose a more direct proof strategy. Focusing on random graph models, we construct a basis of polynomials that is almost orthonormal under $\mathbb{P}$, in precisely those regimes where statistical--computational gaps arise. This almost orthonormal basis not only yields a direct route to establishing low-degree lower bounds, but also allows us to explicitly identify the polynomials that optimize the low-degree criterion. This, in turn, provides insights into the design of optimal polynomial-time algorithms. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach by recovering known low-degree lower bounds, and establishing new ones for problems such as hidden subcliques, stochastic block models, and seriation models.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Carpentier (LMO, CELESTE), Simone Maria Giancola (LMO, CELESTE), Christophe Giraud (LMO, CELESTE), Nicolas Verzelen (MISTEA)

item.title: LoBoost: Model-Native Local Conformal Prediction for Gradient-Boosted Trees
item.description: arXiv:2602.22432v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gradient-boosted decision trees are among the strongest off-the-shelf predictors for tabular regression, but point predictions alone do not quantify uncertainty. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free marginal coverage, yet standard split conformal uses a single global residual quantile and can adapt poorly to heteroscedasticity. We propose LoBoost, a model-native local conformal method that reuses the fitted ensemble's leaf structure to define a multiscale partition of the feature space. Each input is represented by the sequence of leaves it visits along the boosting path, and matching leaf prefixes define nested groups in which residual quantiles are estimated locally. By reusing the predictive structure already learned by the model, LoBoost requires no auxiliary partition or nuisance model, no retraining, and no additional data split beyond standard conformal calibration. Our theory connects the stability of the fitted ensemble and the geometry of its induced cells to local residual-score homogeneity, providing finite-sample coverage-error control and asymptotic pointwise validity as the local calibration size grows and the cells become sufficiently homogeneous. Experiments show a transparent quality-cost trade-off: LoBoost improves over global split conformal on several heterogeneous datasets, but it is not uniformly superior to the adaptive baselines and is not uniformly Pareto-optimal.
item.dc:creator: Vagner Santos, Victor Coscrato, Luben Cabezas, Rafael Izbicki, Thiago Ramos

item.title: The Sampling Complexity of Condorcet Winner Identification in Dueling Bandits
item.description: arXiv:2603.15189v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study best-arm identification in large-scale stochastic dueling bandits under the sole assumption that a Condorcet winner exists, i.e., an arm that wins each noisy pairwise comparison with probability at least $1/2$. We introduce a new identification procedure that exploits the full gap matrix $\Delta_{i,j}=q_{i,j}-\tfrac12$ (where $q_{i,j}$ is the probability that arm $i$ beats arm $j$), rather than only the gaps between the Condorcet winner and the other arms. We derive high-probability, instance-dependent sample-complexity guarantees that (up to logarithmic factors) improve the best known ones by leveraging informative comparisons beyond those involving the winner. We complement these results with matching lower bounds that establish the optimality of our procedures in all regimes. Overall, our results reveal the general form of the sampling complexity, characterized by a trade-off between the cost of locating informative entries and the verification cost required to achieve the desired confidence. In particular, this complexity drastically differs from what is suggested by pure asymptotic results or by procedures that are tailored to Strongly Stochastic Transitive models.
item.dc:creator: El Mehdi Saad (CC-UM6P-Rabat, UM6P), Victor Thuot (MISTEA), Nicolas Verzelen (MISTEA)

item.title: Gaussian mixture models in Hilbert spaces via kernel methods
item.description: arXiv:2605.05996v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern datasets across many disciplines increasingly consist of time-evolving, potentially infinite-dimensional random objects, such as dynamic functional data, which are naturally modeled in Hilbert spaces. In these settings, characterizing probability measures, for example, through densities, can be ill-defined or technically challenging. Motivated by clustering applications, we propose a Gaussian mixture framework for Hilbert-space-valued data based on kernel mean embeddings and develop efficient optimization algorithms for estimation. We establish theoretical guarantees showing that the proposed algorithm is well-defined and that the model yields a dense class of approximations in infinite-dimensional spaces. We evaluate the framework through extensive experiments on diverse data geometries, including $L^2$-functional data and graph signals arising in modern medical applications.
item.dc:creator: Daniel L\'opez-Montero, Antonio \'Alvarez-L\'opez, Marcos Matabuena

item.title: Affine Tracing: A New Paradigm for Probabilistic Linear Solvers
item.description: arXiv:2605.10566v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Probabilistic linear solvers (PLSs) return probability distributions that quantify uncertainty due to limited computation in the solution of linear systems. The literature has traditionally distinguished between Bayesian PLSs, which condition a prior on information obtained from projections of the linear system, and probabilistic iterative methods (PIMs), which lift classical iterative solvers to probability space. In this work we show this dichotomy to be false: Bayesian PLSs are a special case of non-stationary affine PIMs. In addition, we prove that any realistic affine PIM is calibrated. These results motivate a focus on (non-stationary) affine PIMs, but their practical adoption has been limited by the significant manual effort required to implement them. To address this, we introduce affine tracing, an algorithmic framework that automatically constructs a PIM from a standard implementation of an affine iterative method by passing symbolic tracers through the computation to build an affine computational graph. We show how this graph can be transformed to compute posterior covariances, and how equality saturation can be used to perform algebraic simplifications required for computation under specific prior choices. We demonstrate the framework by automatically generating a probabilistic multigrid solver and evaluate its performance in the context of Gaussian process approximation.
item.dc:creator: Disha Hegde, Marvin Pf\"ortner, Jon Cockayne

item.title: Posterior Contraction Rates for Sparse Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Anisotropic Besov Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2605.11652v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study posterior contraction rates for sparse Bayesian Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs) over anisotropic Besov spaces, providing a statistical foundation for KANs from a Bayesian point of view. We show that sparse Bayesian KANs equipped with spike-and-slab-type sparsity priors attain a near-minimax posterior contraction rate. In particular, the contraction rate depends on the intrinsic anisotropic smoothness of the underlying function. Moreover, by placing a hyperprior on a single model-size parameter, the resulting posterior adapts to unknown anisotropic smoothness and still achieves the corresponding near-minimax rate. A distinctive feature of our results, compared with those for standard multilayer perceptrons, is that the KAN depth can be kept fixed: owing to the expressive power of learnable spline edge functions, the required approximation complexity is controlled through the network width, the range and size of the spline grid, and parameter sparsity. Our analysis develops theoretical tools tailored to sparse spline-edge architectures, including approximation and complexity bounds for Bayesian KANs. We then extend to compositional Besov spaces and show that the contraction rates depend on layerwise smoothness and effective dimension of the underlying compositional structure, thereby effectively avoiding the curse of dimensionality. Together, these results advance the theoretical understanding of Bayesian neural networks and establish rigorous Bayesian guarantees for KANs.
item.dc:creator: Jeunghun Oh, Jaeyong Lee, Lizhen Lin, Kyeongwon Lee

item.title: Minimax Rates and Spectral Distillation for Tree Ensembles
item.description: arXiv:2605.11841v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tree ensembles such as random forests (RFs) and gradient boosting machines (GBMs) are among the most widely used supervised learners, yet their theoretical properties remain incompletely understood. We adopt a spectral perspective on these algorithms, with two main contributions. First, we derive minimax-optimal convergence for RF regression, showing that, under mild regularity conditions on tree growth, the eigenvalue decay of the induced kernel operator governs the statistical rate. Second, we exploit this spectral viewpoint to develop compression schemes for tree ensembles. For RFs, leading eigenfunctions of the kernel operator capture the dominant predictive directions; for GBMs, leading singular vectors of the smoother matrix play an analogous role. Learning nonlinear maps for these spectral representations yields distilled models that are orders of magnitude smaller than the originals while maintaining competitive predictive performance. Our methods compare favorably to state of the art algorithms for forest pruning and rule extraction, with applications to resource constrained computing.
item.dc:creator: Binh Duc Vu, David S. Watson

item.title: Factor Augmented High-Dimensional SGD
item.description: arXiv:2605.19291v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a fundamental optimization algorithm widely used in modern machine learning. In this paper, we propose Factor-Augmented SGD (FSGD), a new optimization method that leverages latent factor representations in high-dimensional learning tasks. Unlike standard two-stage dimension reduction approaches that rely on offline representation learning and full data storage, a key novelty of FSGD is that it operates purely on streaming data, making it scalable to large-scale and high-dimensional problems. Furthermore, we establish the first theoretical framework that explicitly incorporates latent factor estimation error into the analysis of SGD, and provide moment convergence in $\ell^s$ norm under decaying step sizes and mini-batch updates. Our results provide a new foundation for employing SGD reliably and scalably in high-dimensional machine learning systems.
item.dc:creator: Shubo Li, Yuefeng Han, Xiufan Yu

item.title: Density-Ratio Losses for Post-Hoc Learning to Defer
item.description: arXiv:2605.19557v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study post-hoc Learning to Defer (L2D) through the lens of ideal distributions: divergence-regularized reweightings of the data distribution under which a model attains low task loss. We define deferral via the density-ratio between a model's and an expert's ideals. Using the reduction from density-ratio estimation to class-probability estimation, we derive the DR CPE losses for post-hoc L2D scorers. Deferral decisions are then made by thresholding the scorer. For KL-based ideal distributions, our deferral rule recovers Chow's rule under the original distribution and a connection to an expert-tilted Bayes posterior---which incorporates the expert's performance---depending on if the ideal distributions are marginal or joint distributions. This leads to two variants of the DR CPE losses, with the joint variant being computationally convenient in practice. We establish consistency properties of the joint DR CPE losses when considering the zero-one task loss and strongly proper composite CPE losses. Experimentally, our approach is competitive compared to common baselines and is more robust across dataset settings. More broadly, our results cast post-hoc L2D as density-ratio estimation between ideal distributions, bridging Chow-style rules, expert comparison, and elucidating connections to related learning settings including anomaly detection.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Soen, Ragnar Thobaben, Joakim Jald\'en, Richard Nock

item.title: Uniform-in-Time Weak Propagation-of-Chaos in Shallow Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2605.22010v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider one-hidden layer neural networks trained in the feature-learning regime using gradient descent, and relate the output of the finite-width network $f_{\hat{\rho}_t^m}$ to its infinite-width counterpart $f_{\rho_t^{MF}}$, which evolves in the mean-field dynamics. While constant-time horizon bounds for $\|f_{\rho_t^{MF}} - f_{\hat{\rho}_t^m}\|$ may be obtained via standard Gr\"onwall estimates, the long-time behavior of the fluctuation is a more delicate matter. Uniform-in-time bounds often rely on (local) strong convexity in the landscape or Logarithmic Sobolev inequalities present in noisy gradient dynamics. In this work, we establish non-asymptotic weak propagation-of-chaos that holds uniformly in time, obtained by exploiting instead the convergence rate of the mean-field deterministic Wasserstein-gradient-flow dynamics. Specifically, denoting by $L_t$ the mean-field excess MSE loss at time $t$ and $m$ the number of neurons, under standard regularity assumptions and the condition $\int_0^\infty L_t^{1/2} dt =O(\log d)$, we obtain the uniform in time bound $\|f_{\rho_t^{MF}}- f_{\hat{\rho}_t^m}\|^2 \lesssim \text{poly}(d) m^{-\min(1,c/6)}$ whenever $L_t \lesssim t^{-c}$. Our result holds in a noiseless setting and does not make any assumptions on the geometry of the landscape near the optimum, and extends seamlessly to other forms of discretization, including finite number of samples and time discretization. A key takeaway of our result is that whenever the convergence rate of the mean-field, population-loss dynamics is faster than $t^{-2}$, we can attain a loss of $\epsilon$ with only $\text{poly}(d/\epsilon)$ neurons, training samples, and GD steps.
item.dc:creator: Margalit Glasgow, Joan Bruna

item.title: Disentangling Forced and Internal Climate Variability in Single Realizations using Dynamic Mode Decomposition with Control
item.description: arXiv:2607.18298v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Separating externally forced trends from internal climate variability is a fundamental challenge in climate science, particularly when analyzing observational records that exist only as a single realization. We show that a single climate realization can be decomposed into forced and internal components by treating external forcing as a dynamical driver within a linear stochastic system, an idea grounded in pullback attractor theory. This addresses a central challenge for climate projection and for detecting and attributing the forced response. Existing single-realization methods rely on linear inverse models (LIMs), which ignore forcing, or linear regression, which omits dynamics. Here we introduce PullbackDMDc, a method grounded in non-autonomous dynamical systems theory and dynamic mode decomposition with control (DMDc), incorporating pullback attractor estimation to decompose a single climate realization into spatial modes and their associated forced and internal components, yielding a physically interpretable picture of the underlying dynamics. After testing on a synthetic system with a known forced response, we illustrate the utility of PullbackDMDc for Earth System Model (ESM) evaluation by applying it to near-surface air temperature and sea-level pressure from reanalysis and four ESM large ensembles. PullbackDMDc estimates the forced response with skill matching or exceeding established baselines and helps select forcing predictors against model-based ground truth. Its internal-variability components reveal that ESMs qualitatively capture interannual and decadal modes while exhibiting systematic differences relative to each other and to observations. Skillful forced-response estimation and a novel decomposition position PullbackDMDc as a practical tool for single-realization climate analysis and ESM evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Mankovich, Andrei Gavrilov, Gustau Camps-Valls

item.title: A Distribution Mapping Approach to Counterfactually Fair Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2608.08743v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to optimize sequential decisions to maximize population-level benefits over time. However, when deployed in high-stakes settings such as healthcare, RL decisions might systematically restrict some subpopulation's access to valuable services in a manner contrary to the values and goals of stakeholders. Counterfactual fairness (CF) offers a promising framework to address this problem based on causal reasoning. This paper develops a data preprocessing algorithm that, when used in tandem with policy learning, enables CF in RL. Our algorithm relies on a novel quantile distribution mapping method for sequentially estimating the counterfactual states and rewards in the data preprocessing step, subsuming common additivity assumptions used for counterfactual prediction as a special case. We theoretically prove that the per-step level of counterfactual unfairness and infinite-horizon suboptimality gap can be bounded under mild regularity conditions. We also empirically test our algorithm in numerical experiments as well as in application to a real-world interventional digital health dataset.
item.dc:creator: Jianhan Zhang, Jitao Wang, John D. Piette, Donglin Zeng, Chengchun Shi, Zhenke Wu

item.title: On Stochastic Continuous-Time Linear System Identification for Adaptive Stabilization
item.description: arXiv:2611.02340v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: System identification studies the canonical problem of reliably learning system-dynamics from state and input trajectories. One of its important applications consists of estimating a feedback gain matrix that can stabilize an unknown system. This paper focuses on the analysis of such adaptive stabilization schemes for multivariate linear time-invariant state-space models. The system instability practically renders trajectories short, i.e., the observed data is notably limited. So, it is crucial to tightly consider effects of \emph{all} involved quantities including length and number of trajectories, dimension, controllability Gramian, and signal-to-noise ratio. We put forward a simple, practical, and reliable relationship between the chance that adaptive stabilization (based on system identification) fails to stabilize the system, in terms of all the above-mentioned quantities. Our findings show that despite exponential effects of all other quantities on failure probability, such effects do not hold for signal-to-noise ratio. More specifically, this study shows that the strength of the excitation signal helps stabilization only \emph{logarithmically}; a very important phenomenon that we explain under the term \emph{signal saturation}.
item.dc:creator: Reza Sadeghi Hafshejani, Mohamad Kazem Shirani Faradonbeh

item.title: Scalable and Calibrated Sampling for Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Model via Stochastic Gradient Markov Chain Monte Carlo
item.description: arXiv:2403.03007v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) are widely used for analyzing correlated data, particularly in large-scale biomedical and social science applications. Scalable Bayesian inference for GLMMs is challenging due to an intractable marginal likelihood and a high computational cost incurred by conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. We develop a stochastic gradient MCMC (SGMCMC) algorithm tailored to GLMMs that enables accurate posterior inference in the large-sample regime. Our approach uses Fisher's identity to construct a (biased) Monte Carlo estimator of the gradient of the marginal log-likelihood, making SGMCMC feasible when direct gradient computation is impossible. We analyze the additional variability, introduced by both data subsampling and gradient approximation, to derive a post-hoc covariance correction that yields properly calibrated posterior uncertainty. We show through simulated studies that the proposed method provides accurate posterior means and variances in settings with a large number of groups, outperforming existing approaches, including control variate methods. We further demonstrate the method's practical utility in an analysis of electronic health records data, where accounting for variance inflation materially changes scientific conclusions.
item.dc:creator: Youngsoo Baek, Andrea Agazzi, Felipe A. Medeiros, Samuel I. Berchuck

item.title: The Star Geometry of Critic-Based Regularizer Learning
item.description: arXiv:2408.16852v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Variational regularization is a classical technique to solve statistical inference tasks and inverse problems, with modern data-driven approaches parameterizing regularizers via deep neural networks showcasing impressive empirical performance. Recent works along these lines learn task-dependent regularizers. This is done by integrating information about the measurements and ground-truth data in an unsupervised, critic-based loss function, where the regularizer attributes low values to likely data and high values to unlikely data. However, there is little theory about the structure of regularizers learned via this process and how it relates to the two data distributions. To make progress on this challenge, we initiate a study of optimizing critic-based loss functions to learn regularizers over a particular family of regularizers: gauges (or Minkowski functionals) of star-shaped bodies. This family contains regularizers that are commonly employed in practice and shares properties with regularizers parameterized by deep neural networks. We specifically investigate critic-based losses derived from variational representations of statistical distances between probability measures. By leveraging tools from star geometry and dual Brunn-Minkowski theory, we illustrate how these losses can be interpreted as dual mixed volumes that depend on the data distribution. This allows us to derive exact expressions for the optimal regularizer in certain cases. Finally, we identify which neural network architectures give rise to such star body gauges and when do such regularizers have favorable properties for optimization. More broadly, this work highlights how the tools of star geometry can aid in understanding the geometry of unsupervised regularizer learning.
item.dc:creator: Oscar Leong, Eliza O'Reilly, Yong Sheng Soh

item.title: Do we really need the Rademacher complexities?
item.description: arXiv:2502.15118v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the fundamental problem of learning with respect to the squared loss in a convex class. In the subgaussian setting, the sharpest known sample complexity bounds are characterised via fixed points associated with the limiting gaussian process. In more general settings (for example, heavier-tailed scenarios) the state-of-the-art bounds rely on localised Rademacher complexities, which are often difficult to control and can be considerably larger than their limiting gaussian counterparts. We show that if one has access to coarse information on the covariance structure of the underlying class, it is possible to derive an upper bound on the sample complexity that matches the state-of-the-art rates in the gaussian setting---even in heavy-tailed regimes. As a consequence, under rather minimal assumptions, learning problems that share the same $L_2$-structure---even those involving heavy-tailed distributions---admit the same upper bound on the sample complexity as if the problem were fully gaussian. This constitutes the first universality result for general convex learning problems. The proof is based on a novel learning procedure, and its performance is studied by combining optimal mean estimation techniques for real-valued random variables with Talagrand's generic chaining method.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Bartl, Shahar Mendelson

item.title: Decentralized Ranking Aggregation via Gossip: Convergence and Robustness
item.description: arXiv:2602.22847v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The concept of ranking aggregation plays a central role in preference analysis, and numerous algorithms for calculating median rankings, often originating in social choice theory, have been documented in the literature, offering theoretical guarantees in a centralized setting, \textit{i.e.}, when all the ranking data to be aggregated can be brought together in a single computing unit. For many technologies (\textit{e.g.} peer-to-peer networks, IoT, multi-agent systems), extending the ability to calculate consensus rankings with guarantees of convergence and resilience to potential contamination in a decentralized setting, when preference data is initially distributed across a communicating network, remains a major methodological challenge. Indeed, in recent years, the literature on decentralized computation has mainly focused on computing or optimizing statistics such as arithmetic means using gossip algorithms. The purpose of this article is precisely to study how to achieve reliable and resilient consensus on collective rankings in a decentralized setting, thereby raising new questions, robustness to corrupted nodes, and scalability through reduced communication costs in particular. The approach proposed and analyzed here relies on the robustness guarantees offered by random gossip communication, which allows autonomous agents to compute a global ranking consensus using local interactions only, without coordination or a central authority.
item.dc:creator: Kerrian Le Caillec, Anna Van Elst, Igor Colin, Stephan Cl\'emen\c{c}on

item.title: Graph Energy Matching: Transport-Aligned Energy-Based Modeling for Graph Generation
item.description: arXiv:2603.23398v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative modeling of discrete data, such as graphs, underpins many scientific and industrial applications, including molecular discovery and materials design. In these domains, probabilistic inference is particularly valuable, as it enables composable generation and principled incorporation of desired constraints, such as structural or functional properties. Energy-based models naturally support this goal by capturing relative likelihoods and enabling composable inference by directly enforcing constraints during inference. However, discrete energy-based models typically struggle with efficient and high-quality sampling, as off-support regions often contain spurious local minima, trapping samplers and causing training instabilities, resulting in a fidelity gap compared to discrete diffusion models. To address this gap, we introduce Graph Energy Matching (GEM), a discrete generative framework inspired by the Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) transport-map optimization perspective. GEM learns a permutation-invariant potential energy that simultaneously guides discrete transport from noise toward high-likelihood graph regions and refines samples within these regions. We further introduce a sampling protocol leveraging an energy-based switching strategy, seamlessly bridging rapid, gradient-guided transport and a local mixing regime for effective exploration. On molecular graph benchmarks, GEM matches or surpasses strong discrete diffusion baselines on most reported metrics. Beyond improving generation quality, GEM's relative likelihood modeling enables targeted exploration, facilitating compositional generation, property-constrained sampling, and interpolation between graphs. Project page: https://michalbalcerak.ai/graph-energy-matching/.
item.dc:creator: Michal Balcerak, Suprosanna Shit, Chinmay Prabhakar, Sebastian Kaltenbach, Michael S. Albergo, Yilun Du, Bjoern Menze

item.title: A unifying view of contrastive learning, importance sampling, and bridge sampling for energy-based models
item.description: arXiv:2604.08116v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the last decades, energy-based models (EBMs) have become an important class of probabilistic models in which a component of the likelihood is intractable and therefore cannot be evaluated explicitly. Consequently, parameter estimation in EBMs is challenging for conventional inference methods. This work is a review paper that brings together these different methodological contributions within a unified framework, highlighting the connections among noise contrastive estimation (NCE), reverse logistic regression (RLR), Bennett's acceptance-ratio (BAR) method, multiple importance sampling (MIS), and bridge sampling within the context of EBMs. Some of them are equivalent under specific conditions. This unified perspective clarifies relationships among existing methods and enables the development of new estimators, with the potential to improve statistical and computational efficiency. Furthermore, this study helps elucidate the success of NCE in terms of its flexibility and robustness, while also identifying scenarios in which its performance can be further improved. Our aim is to provide a self-contained and accessible treatment, with clear and straightforward derivations, that brings together these contributions within a common framework and makes the main results and their underlying ideas understandable to a broader readership. The contribution is twofold. First, this work serves as a comprehensive tutorial for researchers entering the field, introducing the fundamental concepts and derivations. Second, it offers a thorough review for experienced practitioners. The code used in the numerical experiments is available to support the reproducibility of the results.
item.dc:creator: Luca Martino

item.title: Allocating Human Oversight in AI-Enabled Analytics
item.description: arXiv:2604.12497v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence provides low-cost predictions for many analytics tasks, but their reliability and the value of another human label vary across tasks. We study how to allocate a shared human-validation budget when task-level uncertainty is unknown and each acquired label informs both estimation and subsequent allocation. For known difficulty levels, the benchmark follows a cost-adjusted Neyman rule that accounts for task importance and label cost. Within our Tuned Rectification-Difficulty framework, we develop an upper-confidence-bound policy that jointly learns the correction coefficients of tuned prediction-powered inference and the resulting difficulties from paired human labels and predictions, and establish an allocation-regret guarantee for the confidence-radius policy. In synthetic experiments and a real digital-twin survey with 68 tasks and over 2,000 respondents, our method closes most of the gap to the oracle on the allocation objective. It matches the estimation error of uniform allocation with up to 22.7% and 4.5% fewer human labels, respectively. The same allocation structure extends beyond scalar means to vector-valued decision models, including regression and choice/conjoint estimation, by replacing the scalar residual variance with a scalarized sandwich covariance. The value of AI depends not only on model accuracy but also on the operational policy that targets human oversight where it matters most.
item.dc:creator: Zikun Ye, Jiameng Lyu, Rui Tao

item.title: Minimax Optimal Estimation of Transport-Growth Pairs in Unbalanced Optimal Transport
item.description: arXiv:2605.08705v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unbalanced optimal transport extends classical optimal transport to measures with different total masses, but statistical guarantees for estimation of the transport map and the growth map remain limited. We study unbalanced optimal transport with quadratic cost and Kullback-Leibler marginal penalties and argue that the natural target of estimation is a transport-growth pair. Consequently, we develop two estimators for the transport-growth pair under two setups: a nearest-neighbor estimator for transporting between general densities, and a kernel-based estimator for transporting between smooth densities. We prove that the kernel-based estimator achieves the minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor by deriving a matching lower bound on the minimax risk. Our main technical contribution is a reduction of estimation to a stability bound on the unbalanced optimal transport value. This bound controls the transport map and growth map risks through the duality gap of the true dual potentials for the estimated measures. These results provide a statistical foundation for estimation of the transport-growth pair in unbalanced optimal transport.
item.dc:creator: Donlapark Ponnoprat, Noboru Isobe, Masaaki Imaizumi

item.title: Variance Reduction for Gradients from Diffusion Teachers
item.description: arXiv:2605.21489v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pretrained diffusion models serve as frozen teachers for pipelines such as text-to-3D, single-step distillation, and data attribution. The teacher gradients these pipelines consume are expectations over noise levels and Gaussian noise, estimated by Monte Carlo (MC). Each MC draw requires expensive upstream work (rendering, simulation, encoding), so estimator variance dominates compute cost. We introduce CARV, a compute-aware variance-accounting framework that casts these gradients as a classical two-stage sampling problem with asymmetric per-level costs. This motivates a hierarchical MC estimator that amortizes each expensive upstream computation by reusing it across cheap diffusion draws, with within-unit variance further reduced by timestep importance sampling (IS) and stratified inverse-CDF sampling. CARV delivers 2 to 3x effective compute multipliers on text-to-3D and data attribution without changing the objective. In text-to-3D, reuse provides most of the gain and IS with stratification adds about 25%. In single-step distillation, the same techniques cut gradient variance by an order of magnitude but do not improve downstream FID, marking the regime where MC variance is no longer the bottleneck.
item.dc:creator: Jesse Bettencourt, Xindi Wu, Matan Atzmon, James Lucas, Jonathan Lorraine

item.title: Total Variation Distance Estimation in Autoregressive Models
item.description: arXiv:2607.19510v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern LLM deployments use a number of implementation choices and inference optimizations (e.g., batching, custom kernels, and quantization) on top of fixed weights, so two engines serving "the same model" can produce meaningfully different distributions. We study the problem of estimating the total variation (TV) distance between two length-$n$ autoregressive distributions to additive error $\varepsilon$, under three access models. (1) Under sample access, we use $\widetilde{O}(n^2 K/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, where $K$ is the maximum support of the next-token distribution.
